justification: Committed to B. The passage puts the lifting force in the shallow mats: “In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones – where the slab cools after sunset and moisture condenses on its underside … her team found dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year”, and Askerholt says “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone.” A fails because she does settle the question rather than failing to; C overstates “there was almost nothing alive” into “entirely without roots”; D’s cut anchoring roots are never mentioned anywhere in the text.

Committed to D. The five are explicitly characterised: “They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows, and the roots had evidently found it worth living in.” A is contradicted twice – “The crates, not the soil, carry the weight of the traffic above” and root mats “riding clear over the crates beneath” (crates intact). B describes the separate single street where “a water main was renewed halfway along it”, which “failed and taught nobody anything”. C is directly contradicted by “The five had one thing in common.”

Committed to A. The closing paragraph is explicit that the good streets are only inferred from the surface: “The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones”, and Askerholt adds “We are reading the flags, not the roots … For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength.” B is contradicted by “stayed within tolerance” plus the recorded “four millimetres” (movement exists, it is merely tolerable); C is an absolute the passage pointedly refuses; D is not addressed.

Committed to B. Fearnbeck predicted “The roots will cross the crates and settle in the bedding”, and on five streets the survey “found exactly what Fearnbeck had said it would find”, but on twenty-five it did not. The writer then judges in her own voice: “Askerholt’s group had thought his worry overdone. On the five streets the case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not” – vindicated on one point, unvindicated in general. A and C each take only one half of that sentence; D fails because “the case is fairly won … on the twenty-five it is not” is the writer adjudicating, not abstaining.

Committed to C. The text does two things and only two: it explains the mechanism – “The slab shades the ground, waters it every clear night and lets it breathe. It builds the very thing that lifts it” – and then reports how the root-cell remedy fared across “Thirty-one streets … rebuilt on cells” over seven years. A takes only the framing (“compensation for trips over lifted paving costs more each year”); B’s “finally beat” is contradicted by “The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to”; D is not addressed at all.

Committed to C. The frame is “it quietly takes its ___(1)___ on the general mood”, and only “toll” completes the fixed collocation take its toll on, which also carries the required sense of slow cumulative damage matching “quietly”. “price” and “cost” are exacted or paid, not “taken … on” something; “charge” takes no such pattern at all.

Committed to D. The contrastive “but” and the target sentence set the surface against the intent: “The tone is light, but nobody misreads it; beneath the sponge the message is ___(2)___, and it is aimed at certain chairs.” Only “pointed” supplies the required sharpness-with-a-target that “aimed at certain chairs” demands. “relaxed” and “amused” restate the light tone and so destroy the contrast; “spirited” means lively, which is neither the contrast nor a property a written notice’s hidden meaning can have here.

Committed to A. “you cannot hold the moral high ___(3)___ and a dripping brush at the same time” is the fixed idiom the moral high ground, and the joke depends on the reader recognising it verbatim. “horse” belongs to a different idiom (get on one’s high horse) and cannot be held; “field” and “floor” produce no English phrase in this frame.

Committed to B. The two sentences are a wait and its resolution: “So the kitchen waits. ___(4)___, somebody cracks – nearly always the same somebody”, which requires the temporal “Eventually”. “Similarly” asserts a parallel that the preceding sentence does not offer; “Presumably” hedges a claim the writer immediately details as known fact; “Ironically” would need a reversal, and someone cracking after a wait is the expected outcome, not a reversal.

Committed to C. “most kitchens ___(5)___ an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor” takes strike, the standard verb of strike a balance, and “uneasy balance” is its most common modifier. “cast”, “deal” and “land” each collocate with other objects (a vote, a blow, a deal, a punch) but none governs “a balance” in English.

Committed to A. Slaking is described directly: “Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl” – seething, cracking and crumbling to a fine white powder, which A paraphrases exactly. C reverses the chemistry: it is heat, not water, that expels the carbon dioxide (“När kalksten hettas upp till omkring tusen grader driver värmen ut koldioxiden ur stenen”). B’s moulds appear nowhere; D is contradicted because the stone disintegrates and still needs sand (“som blandad med sand ger murbruk”).

Committed to D. The organisation paragraph is unambiguous: “En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och brändes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar som sköt till var sin andel ved, turades om vid elden och delade den färdiga kalken efter insats.” A is contradicted by that same first sentence; B’s visiting professional burners are never mentioned – burning was “böndernas sak”; C is contradicted by “Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu.”

Committed to B. Both halves of B are stated: the trade was a significant side income – “för många hushåll var ugnen den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter” – and its traces survive – “ett sjuttiotal ugnsrester bara i Klyvinge med grannsocknar: låga, övervuxna rösen av rödbränd sten”. A inverts the priority (“Fram för allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen”, with only “något” reaching the fields); C overstates “för många hushåll” into a collapse of the whole rural cash economy; D is contradicted by “Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer”.

Committed to C. The remains are described as successive rather than simultaneous: “inte sällan flera i rad utmed samma sluttning, äldre ugnar som övergivits när skogen omkring dem huggits ut och ersatts av en yngre ugn längre bort” – so a count of surviving remains overstates how many were in operation at any one time. D is directly contradicted by “Hur gamla de äldsta lämningarna är går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning”; A makes a national comparison the text never offers; B compares Klyvinge with its neighbouring parishes, which the text also never does.

The passage locates the lifting force in the shallow root mat: “In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones – where the slab cools after sunset and moisture condenses on its underside … her team found dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year”, and Askerholt herself says “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone.” A rejects the text outright — she did settle where the force comes from. C is the strongest near-miss but overstates: the text says only that half a metre down “there was almost nothing alive”, which is a hedge, not ‘entirely without roots’. D (cut anchoring roots) is never mentioned anywhere in the passage.

“The five had one thing in common. They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows, and the roots had evidently found it worth living in.” That is D verbatim in substance. C is directly contradicted by “The five had one thing in common”. B is the deliberate trap: the water main belongs to a different street entirely — “One street failed and taught nobody anything: a water main was renewed halfway along it” — and is counted separately from the five. A (crates giving way) is never claimed; the text says the crates carry the traffic load by design.

The final paragraph is built to imply exactly A: “The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones”, and Askerholt’s “We are reading the flags, not the roots … For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength.” B is the hardest rival but fails on the text’s own wording — the celled flags “have stayed within tolerance”, and the closing gauge reading is “four millimetres”, i.e. movement inside tolerance, not ‘not shifted at all’. C (“never”) is an absolute the passage explicitly refuses, and D (trees drawing water from beneath the road) is nowhere stated — the cells are said only to move the damp, aired horizon down and away from the stones.

The writer delivers her own split verdict: “Askerholt’s group had thought his worry overdone. On the five streets the case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not.” “The case” must be Fearnbeck’s — on the five the treatment failed, so it cannot be Askerholt’s that is “fairly won” there — so he is vindicated on five streets and unvindicated on twenty-five: right on one point, not borne out overall. A is refuted by “the case is fairly won” on the five; C is refuted by “on the twenty-five it is not”. D is the strongest rival, since the piece is otherwise scrupulously even-handed (“Not everyone was persuaded”), but “fairly won … it is not” is an authorial adjudication, so she does take a position.

The text opens with why flags rise (“A mature lime can lift a fifty-kilo flag by several centimetres in a decade”, then Askerholt’s shallow-root mechanism) and spends the second half on one city’s trial of root cells and its mixed seven-year result. A is only the first paragraph’s framing detail about insurers and compensation. B is contradicted by the unresolved ending — “on the twenty-five it is not” and “The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to.” D (replacing trees with smaller species) is never raised at all.

The fixed collocation is ‘take its toll on’: “it quietly takes its ___(1)___ on the general mood” needs a noun that combines with “takes its” and “on”. A ‘price’ and D ‘cost’ are the closest semantically — both name a burden — but English pays a price and counts a cost; neither is “taken” on something. B ‘charge’ fails both the idiom and the sense.

The clause turns on a concession: “The tone is light, but nobody misreads it; beneath the sponge the message is ___(2)___, and it is aimed at certain chairs.” “But” and “aimed at certain chairs” demand something sharp and directed, which is ‘pointed’. A ‘relaxed’ and C ‘amused’ restate the light tone the “but” is contrasting against, so they kill the sentence’s logic; B ‘spirited’ is lively rather than targeted and leaves “aimed at certain chairs” unexplained.

“you cannot hold the moral high ___(3)___ and a dripping brush at the same time” is the frozen idiom ‘the moral high ground’. D ‘floor’ is the tempting near-miss because one does ‘hold the floor’, but ‘the moral high floor’ is not English; B ‘field’ and C ‘horse’ belong to other idioms (‘high horse’ is ridden or got down from, never held, and takes no ‘moral high’ premodifier).

“So the kitchen waits. ___(4)___, somebody cracks – nearly always the same somebody” sets up a period of waiting that ends, so the gap wants a temporal marker: ‘Eventually’. A ‘Similarly’ asserts a parallel with the preceding sentence that does not exist. C ‘Presumably’ hedges a fact the columnist reports as observed and recurring. D ‘Ironically’ is the strongest rival — there is mild irony in the most fastidious person doing the work — but it leaves ‘the kitchen waits’ hanging with no resolution in time.

“most kitchens ___(5)___ an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor” takes the standard collocation ‘strike a balance’. B ‘deal’ is the nearest trap since one strikes a deal, but ‘deal a balance’ is not English; A ‘cast’ and D ‘land’ have no balance collocation either (‘land’ would need an object like a job or a punch).

Texten beskriver släckningen så här: “Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl” — vilket är just A:s ‘fräste sönder till ett vitt pulver’. C is the sharpest trap and is contradicted by the previous sentence, where it is the heat, not the water, that expels the carbon dioxide: “När kalksten hettas upp till omkring tusen grader driver värmen ut koldioxiden ur stenen”. D fails because the slaked lime is a powder that still has to be “blandad med sand” to give mortar, and B (casting in moulds) appears nowhere in the text.

“En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och brändes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar som sköt till var sin andel ved, turades om vid elden och delade den färdiga kalken efter insats.” That is D. A is contradicted by “för stor för ett enskilt hushåll”; C is contradicted by “Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu”; B (visiting professional burners) is the most plausible-sounding invention but the text names only neighbours organised in an ugnslag with a karvstock for reckoning.

B unites two claims the text makes explicitly: “för många hushåll var ugnen den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter”, and the surviving traces — “ett sjuttiotal ugnsrester bara i Klyvinge med grannsocknar: låga, övervuxna rösen av rödbränd sten”. C is the hardest rival, and it is an overreach: the text says the kiln was the only cash income for many households, never that rural money economy would have collapsed without it. A is contradicted by “Framför allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen” with only “något” reaching the fields; D is contradicted by “Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer” — it was firewood and the market that ran out, not the stone.

The inference is licensed by the sequencing of the remains: “inte sällan flera i rad utmed samma sluttning, äldre ugnar som övergivits när skogen omkring dem huggits ut och ersatts av en yngre ugn längre bort” — so the seventy-odd remains accumulated successively and cannot all have burned at once. D is flatly contradicted by “Hur gamla de äldsta lämningarna är går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning.” A (largest lime seller in the country) and B (ceased earlier than in neighbouring parishes) are comparisons the text never makes; the neighbouring parishes are counted together with Klyvinge, not against it.
